claim: Both male rodents and humans exhibit increased pain sensitivity in environments recently associated with a single painful experience.
source: Contextual cues, which comprise the environment in which events occur, were recently described as a critical regulator of pain memory; both male rodents and humans exhibit increased pain sensitivity in environments recently associated with a single painful experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Martin et al., 2019) as indicated in the manuscript text.

claim: When re-exposed to the noxious stimulus in a familiar environment, both male and female mice exhibited context-dependent conditioned analgesia.
source: When re-exposed to the noxious stimulus in a familiar environment, both male and female mice exhibited context-dependent conditioned analgesia, a phenomenon mediated by endogenous opioid signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Context-dependent conditioned analgesia is mediated by endogenous opioid signaling.
source: When re-exposed to the noxious stimulus in a familiar environment, both male and female mice exhibited context-dependent conditioned analgesia, a phenomenon mediated by endogenous opioid signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that naloxone (an opioid antagonist) blocks conditioned analgesia, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: When expecting the presentation of a painful stimulus in a given context, males exhibited conditioned hypersensitivity.
source: However, when expecting the presentation of a painful stimulus in a given context, males exhibited conditioned hypersensitivity whereas females exhibited endogenous opioid-mediated conditioned analgesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B showing male mice exhibited lower withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired context on day 4 despite receiving vehicle injections.

claim: When expecting the presentation of a painful stimulus in a given context, females exhibited endogenous opioid-mediated conditioned analgesia.
source: However, when expecting the presentation of a painful stimulus in a given context, males exhibited conditioned hypersensitivity whereas females exhibited endogenous opioid-mediated conditioned analgesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C and 4E showing that naloxone treatment decreased withdrawal thresholds in acid-trained female mice on day 4.

claim: Pain perception can be modified through psychological association with environmental cues.
source: These results are evidence that pain perception and engagement of endogenous opioid systems can be modified through their psychological association with environmental cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing context-dependent changes in pain behaviors across multiple experiments.

claim: Engagement of endogenous opioid systems can be modified through psychological association with environmental cues.
source: These results are evidence that pain perception and engagement of endogenous opioid systems can be modified through their psychological association with environmental cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that naloxone blocks conditioned analgesia, indicating that environmental cues trigger endogenous opioid release.

claim: Chronic pain development may involve the generalization and strengthening of acute pain memories.
source: Chronic pain development may involve the generalization and strengthening of acute pain memories (Moseley and Vlaeyen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moseley and Vlaeyen, 2015.

claim: Neuronal encoding of painful stimuli (nociception) is an evolutionarily conserved, unconditioned response generated upon exposure to a tissue-damaging unconditioned stimulus.
source: Neuronal encoding of painful stimuli, known as nociception, is an evolutionarily conserved, unconditioned response (UCR) generated upon exposure to a tissue-damaging unconditioned stimulus (UCS).
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about nociception.

claim: Pairings of the painful UCS with external cues can eventually lead to the development of a conditioned response elicited by the CS alone.
source: Pairings of the painful UCS with external cues can eventually lead to the development of a conditioned response (CR) elicited by the CS alone.
evidence: This claim is based on established principles of Pavlovian conditioning.

claim: Pavlov was the first to describe the process through which a biologically irrelevant stimulus could come to exert control over physiological processes.
source: Pavlov, 2010, was the first to describe the process through which a biologically irrelevant stimulus could come to exert control over physiological processes in a way that allows the organism to prepare for the upcoming disruption of homeostasis produced by the UCS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pavlov, 2010.

claim: When heroin was administered in a novel context, a lethal dose killed 64.3% of animals.
source: When administered in a novel context, this dose of heroin killed 64.3% of animals; the same amount of heroin administered in the familiar context decreased the death rate by ~50% such that only 32.4% of animals died.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 1982.

claim: The same amount of heroin administered in the familiar context decreased the death rate by ~50% such that only 32.4% of animals died.
source: When administered in a novel context, this dose of heroin killed 64.3% of animals; the same amount of heroin administered in the familiar context decreased the death rate by ~50% such that only 32.4% of animals died.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 1982.

claim: The familiar environment served as a CS that predicted upcoming heroin administration, thereby initiating internal processes associated with drug tolerance.
source: Similar to the CR first reported by Pavlov, 2010, this work suggested that the familiar environment served as a CS that predicted upcoming heroin administration, thereby initiating internal processes associated with drug tolerance.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the Siegel et al., 1982 study results.

claim: Context can exert control over learned behaviors related to fear and anxiety.
source: It is also well documented that context can exert control over learned behaviors related to fear and anxiety (Bouton and Bolles, 1979) as well as over instrumental and choice behaviors (Trask and Bouton, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bouton and Bolles, 1979.

claim: Context can exert control over instrumental and choice behaviors.
source: It is also well documented that context can exert control over learned behaviors related to fear and anxiety (Bouton and Bolles, 1979) as well as over instrumental and choice behaviors (Trask and Bouton, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Trask and Bouton, 2014.

claim: Context was found to influence pain behaviors in male mice and humans after a single conditioning trial.
source: Recently, context was found to influence pain behaviors in male mice and humans after a single conditioning trial (Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2019.

claim: Both male mice and men exhibited stress-induced hyperalgesia if tested in an environment previously associated with a painful stimulus.
source: Both male mice and men exhibited stress-induced hyperalgesia if tested in an environment previously associated with a painful stimulus (Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2019.

claim: Male mice avoided the environment previously associated with a noxious UCS in a place avoidance task.
source: Similarly, in a place avoidance task, male mice avoided the environment previously associated with this same noxious UCS (Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2019.

claim: Neither female mice nor women exhibited conditioned hypersensitivity, conditioned place aversion, or context-dependent increases in circulating stress hormones.
source: Neither female mice nor women exhibited conditioned hypersensitivity, conditioned place aversion, or context-dependent increases in circulating stress hormones in these experiments, suggesting that context did not impact nociceptive signaling in females as it did in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2019.

claim: Following fear conditioning in which a CS predicts an aversive shock outcome, animals exhibited increased pain tolerance in the environment where fear conditioning occurred.
source: In general, those studies found that following fear conditioning in which a CS predicts an aversive shock outcome, animals exhibited increased pain tolerance (i.e., conditioned hypoalgesia) in the environment, or context, where fear conditioning occurred (Fanselow and Helmstetter, 1988; Harris and Westbrook, 1994; Harris and Westbrook, 1995; Helmstetter and Fanselow, 1987; Watkins et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: On day 1, female mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle chamber.
source: On day 1, female mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN (i.e., increased pain in the hindpaw following administration of a painful stimulus in the abdomen) in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle chamber (p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: On day 4, female hindpaw sensitivity was greater in the vehicle-paired context than the acid-paired context despite animals receiving IP injection of 0.9% acetic acid prior to being placed into either chamber.
source: However, on day 4, female hindpaw sensitivity was greater in the vehicle-paired context than the acid-paired context (p = 0.001) despite the fact that animals received IP injection of 0.9% acetic acid prior to being placed into either chamber.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: Male mice exhibited similar levels of hindpaw mechanical sensitivity in both the acid- and vehicle-paired contexts on day 1 and day 4.
source: Male mice (Figure 1B) exhibited similar levels of hindpaw mechanical sensitivity in both the acid- and vehicle-paired contexts on day 1 (p = 0.91) and day 4 (p = 0.29), suggesting that associative learning did not enable environmental control of pain sensitivity in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B and statistical analysis.

claim: Following acid injection on day 1, females exhibited hyperalgesic DCN whereas males did not.
source: Following acid injection on day 1, females exhibited hyperalgesic DCN whereas males did not (p < 0.001; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D and statistical analysis.

claim: Hindpaw sensitivity in female mice was greater than in male mice following an IP injection of 0.9% acetic acid and placement into the vehicle-paired chamber on day 4.
source: Similarly, hindpaw sensitivity in female mice was greater than in male mice following an IP injection of 0.9% acetic acid and placement into the vehicle-paired chamber on day 4 (p = 0.045), even though both sexes exhibited higher mechanical sensitivity in this chamber on day 4 as compared to day 1 (males: p = 0.003; females: p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 and statistical analysis.

claim: When injected with acid and placed into the acid-paired context on day 4, females exhibited less hindpaw sensitivity than males.
source: However, when injected with acid and placed into the acid-paired context on day 4, females exhibited less hindpaw sensitivity than males (p = 0.011; Figure 1D); male hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were lower in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 as compared to day 1 (p = 0.002), whereas female hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were higher in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 (p = 0.006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D and statistical analysis.

claim: Male hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were lower in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 as compared to day 1.
source: However, when injected with acid and placed into the acid-paired context on day 4, females exhibited less hindpaw sensitivity than males (p = 0.011; Figure 1D); male hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were lower in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 as compared to day 1 (p = 0.002), whereas female hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were higher in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 (p = 0.006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D and statistical analysis.

claim: Female hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were higher in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1.
source: However, when injected with acid and placed into the acid-paired context on day 4, females exhibited less hindpaw sensitivity than males (p = 0.011; Figure 1D); male hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were lower in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 as compared to day 1 (p = 0.002), whereas female hindpaw withdrawal thresholds were higher in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 (p = 0.006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D and statistical analysis.

claim: Context did not alter reflexive writhing behaviors in either sex on day 4.
source: Notably, context did not alter reflexive writhing behaviors in either sex on day 4 (Figure 1G), despite blocking the hyperalgesic DCN observed in von Frey testing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Prior experience, or pain memories associated with a specific environment, induce a conditioned compensatory response that decreases hyperalgesic DCN only in female mice.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that prior experience, or pain memories associated with a specific environment, induce a conditioned compensatory response that decreases hyperalgesic DCN only in female mice.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 1.

claim: Male mice do not develop conditioned place aversion unless trained with doses of acetic acid >0.3%.
source: Previous studies have also shown that male mice do not develop conditioned place aversion unless trained with doses of acetic acid >0.3% (Bagdas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bagdas et al., 2016.

claim: Males exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired chamber on day 1 relative to the vehicle-paired chamber.
source: As before, planned comparisons were conducted to assess differences both between- and within-groups. In contrast to the results from the previous experiment, males exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired chamber on day 1 (p = 0.006; Figure 2B) and conditioned analgesia in this chamber on day 4 (p = 0.006) relative to the vehicle-paired chamber.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and statistical analysis.

claim: Males exhibited conditioned analgesia in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 relative to the vehicle-paired chamber.
source: As before, planned comparisons were conducted to assess differences both between- and within-groups. In contrast to the results from the previous experiment, males exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired chamber on day 1 (p = 0.006; Figure 2B) and conditioned analgesia in this chamber on day 4 (p = 0.006) relative to the vehicle-paired chamber.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and statistical analysis.

claim: Female mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired chamber on day 1 relative to the vehicle-paired chamber.
source: A similar pattern was observed in females (Figure 2C); relative to the vehicle-paired chamber, female mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired chamber on day 1 (p = 0.003), and conditioned analgesia in this chamber as early as day 2 in some animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but by day 4 in all mice (Figure 2C; p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C and statistical analysis.

claim: Female mice exhibited conditioned analgesia in the acid-paired chamber as early as day 2 in some animals.
source: A similar pattern was observed in females (Figure 2C); relative to the vehicle-paired chamber, female mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired chamber on day 1 (p = 0.003), and conditioned analgesia in this chamber as early as day 2 in some animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but by day 4 in all mice (Figure 2C; p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The magnitude of hyperalgesic DCN exhibited following 0.9% acetic acid injection on day 1 was greater in females than males.
source: Although the magnitude of hyperalgesic DCN exhibited following 0.9% acetic acid injection on day 1 was greater in females than males (p = 0.024; Figure 2D), hindpaw mechanical thresholds in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 were not significantly different between the sexes (p = 0.078).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and statistical analysis.

claim: Hindpaw mechanical thresholds in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 were not significantly different between the sexes.
source: Although the magnitude of hyperalgesic DCN exhibited following 0.9% acetic acid injection on day 1 was greater in females than males (p = 0.024; Figure 2D), hindpaw mechanical thresholds in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 were not significantly different between the sexes (p = 0.078).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and statistical analysis.

claim: Males exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the vehicle-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1.
source: In planned comparisons that assessed behavior across days, males exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the vehicle-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 (p < 0.001) but did not exhibit conditioned analgesia in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 relative to day 1 (Figure 2D; p = 0.42).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and statistical analysis.

claim: Males did not exhibit conditioned analgesia in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 relative to day 1.
source: In planned comparisons that assessed behavior across days, males exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the vehicle-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 (p < 0.001) but did not exhibit conditioned analgesia in the acid-paired chamber on day 4 relative to day 1 (Figure 2D; p = 0.42).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and statistical analysis.

claim: Females demonstrated both hyperalgesic DCN in the vehicle-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 and conditioned analgesia in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1.
source: This was not the case for females as they demonstrated both hyperalgesic DCN in the vehicle-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 (p = 0.002) and conditioned analgesia in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 (Figure 2D; p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and statistical analysis.

claim: Males exhibited more writhing behavior in the acid-paired context than the vehicle-paired context on day 1.
source: Planned comparisons revealed that males exhibited more writhing behavior in the acid-paired context than the vehicle-paired context on day 1 (Figure 2E, p < 0.001) but not day 4 (p = 0.56).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E and statistical analysis.

claim: Females exhibited more writhing in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle-associated context on day 1.
source: Although females exhibited more writhing in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle-associated context on day 1 (Figure 2F; p < 0.001), the opposite was observed on day 4 (p = 0.03); females exhibited less writhing in the acid-associated context than the vehicle-associated context despite receiving identical 0.9% acetic acid injections before being placed into each.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F and statistical analysis.

claim: On day 4, females exhibited less writhing in the acid-associated context than the vehicle-associated context despite receiving identical 0.9% acetic acid injections before being placed into each.
source: Although females exhibited more writhing in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle-associated context on day 1 (Figure 2F; p < 0.001), the opposite was observed on day 4 (p = 0.03); females exhibited less writhing in the acid-associated context than the vehicle-associated context despite receiving identical 0.9% acetic acid injections before being placed into each.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F and statistical analysis.

claim: Both sexes exhibited less writhing in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 suggesting either the development of acetic acid tolerance or conditioned analgesia.
source: However, both sexes exhibited less writhing in the acid-paired context on day 4 relative to day 1 suggesting either the development of acetic acid tolerance or conditioned analgesia (Figure 2G; males: p = 0.043; females: p = 0.047).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2G and statistical analysis.

claim: Both sexes are able to develop conditioned analgesia if trained with strong UCS, but the magnitude of this phenomenon may differ between the sexes with females being especially sensitive to this type of learning.
source: Considering these data, and the fact that male mice had higher withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired context on day 4 as compared to the vehicle-paired context, we conclude that both sexes are able to develop conditioned analgesia if trained with strong UCS, but the magnitude of this phenomenon may differ between the sexes with females being especially sensitive to this type of learning.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: Acid-trained animals exhibited hyperalgesic DCN relative to vehicle-trained animals on day 1.
source: Planned comparisons found that similar to observations in the acid-paired context in our within-subject experiment (Figure 2), acid-trained animals exhibited hyperalgesic DCN relative to vehicle-trained animals on day 1 (p < 0.001) and conditioned analgesia relative to vehicle-trained animals on day 4 (p = 0.008; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: Acid-trained animals exhibited conditioned analgesia relative to vehicle-trained animals on day 4.
source: Planned comparisons found that similar to observations in the acid-paired context in our within-subject experiment (Figure 2), acid-trained animals exhibited hyperalgesic DCN relative to vehicle-trained animals on day 1 (p < 0.001) and conditioned analgesia relative to vehicle-trained animals on day 4 (p = 0.008; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: Corticosterone levels were similar between acid- and vehicle-trained mice.
source: Corticosterone levels were similar between acid- and vehicle-trained mice (Figure 3C; t(14) = 0.56, p = 0.58) suggesting that the observed behaviors were likely not forms of stress-induced analgesia or hyperalgesia in the acid- and vehicle-trained mice, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C and statistical analysis.

claim: The observed behaviors were likely not forms of stress-induced analgesia or hyperalgesia in the acid- and vehicle-trained mice.
source: Corticosterone levels were similar between acid- and vehicle-trained mice (Figure 3C; t(14) = 0.56, p = 0.58) suggesting that the observed behaviors were likely not forms of stress-induced analgesia or hyperalgesia in the acid- and vehicle-trained mice, respectively.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the corticosterone data.

claim: Naloxone pre-treatment had no effect on the hyperalgesic DCN exhibited by vehicle-trained animals on day 4.
source: We found no evidence for any effect of naloxone pre-treatment on the hyperalgesic DCN exhibited by vehicle-trained animals on day 4 (Figure 3E; p = 0.64), but it successfully blocked the conditioned analgesia exhibited by acid-trained mice on day 4 (Figure 3E; p < 0.001); the mechanical withdrawal thresholds of naloxone injected acid-trained mice were similar to those exhibited by vehicle-trained mice after their first exposure to acetic acid.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E and statistical analysis.

claim: Naloxone successfully blocked the conditioned analgesia exhibited by acid-trained mice on day 4.
source: We found no evidence for any effect of naloxone pre-treatment on the hyperalgesic DCN exhibited by vehicle-trained animals on day 4 (Figure 3E; p = 0.64), but it successfully blocked the conditioned analgesia exhibited by acid-trained mice on day 4 (Figure 3E; p < 0.001); the mechanical withdrawal thresholds of naloxone injected acid-trained mice were similar to those exhibited by vehicle-trained mice after their first exposure to acetic acid.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E and statistical analysis.

claim: Naloxone blocked conditioned analgesia to a similar extent in male and female acid-trained mice.
source: This analysis revealed a main effect of drug, F(1, 20) = 31.62, MSE = 3.14, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.61, but no main effect of sex nor an interaction between the two (Fs < 1), suggesting that naloxone blocked conditioned analgesia to a similar extent in male (vehicle vs. naloxone; p = 0.005) and female (vehicle vs. naloxone; p < 0.001) acid-trained mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F and statistical analysis.

claim: Vehicle-treated acid-trained male mice showed a modest reduction in writhing from day 1 to day 4.
source: Similar to results in the within-subject experiment, vehicle-treated acid-trained male mice showed a modest reduction in writhing from day 1 to day 4 (Figure 3G; p = 0.12), hinting at either the development of acid tolerance or conditioned analgesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3G and statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction in writhing behavior was even more pronounced in naloxone-treated acid-trained male animals.
source: This reduction in writhing behavior was even more pronounced in naloxone-treated acid-trained animals, suggesting that decreases in reflexive writhing behaviors are not a result of increased endogenous opioid signaling in males (Figure 3G; p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3G and statistical analysis.

claim: Decreases in reflexive writhing behaviors are not a result of increased endogenous opioid signaling in males.
source: This reduction in writhing behavior was even more pronounced in naloxone-treated acid-trained animals, suggesting that decreases in reflexive writhing behaviors are not a result of increased endogenous opioid signaling in males (Figure 3G; p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the writhing data in naloxone-treated males.

claim: Vehicle-treated, acid-trained females exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 4 relative to day 1.
source: Alternatively, vehicle-treated, acid-trained females exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 4 relative to day 1 (Figure 3H; p = 0.003), an effect that was blocked by naloxone treatment on day 4 (Figure 3E; p = 0.51).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3H and statistical analysis.

claim: Naloxone treatment blocked conditioned analgesia in acid-trained females on day 4.
source: Alternatively, vehicle-treated, acid-trained females exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 4 relative to day 1 (Figure 3H; p = 0.003), an effect that was blocked by naloxone treatment on day 4 (Figure 3E; p = 0.51).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3H and statistical analysis.

claim: Both male and female mice recruit the endogenous opioid system as a compensatory response to repeated acetic acid administration.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that both male and female mice recruit the endogenous opioid system as a compensatory response to repeated acetic acid administration, however the extent to which this system influences UCS-induced pain behaviors may differ between the sexes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: The extent to which the endogenous opioid system influences UCS-induced pain behaviors may differ between the sexes.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that both male and female mice recruit the endogenous opioid system as a compensatory response to repeated acetic acid administration, however the extent to which this system influences UCS-induced pain behaviors may differ between the sexes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: Male mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle-paired context on day 1.
source: Male mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle-paired context on day 1 (Figure 4B; p < 0.001), and, similar to the conditioned hypersensitivity previously reported after single exposure to a noxious UCS (Martin et al., 2019), context-dependent hypersensitivity in the absence of the UCS on day 4 (Figure 4B; p = 0.027).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B and statistical analysis.

claim: Male mice exhibited context-dependent hypersensitivity in the absence of the UCS on day 4.
source: Male mice exhibited hyperalgesic DCN in the acid-paired context relative to the vehicle-paired context on day 1 (Figure 4B; p < 0.001), and, similar to the conditioned hypersensitivity previously reported after single exposure to a noxious UCS (Martin et al., 2019), context-dependent hypersensitivity in the absence of the UCS on day 4 (Figure 4B; p = 0.027).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B and statistical analysis.

claim: Male hindpaw withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired chamber were lower than thresholds recorded in the vehicle-paired chamber on day 4, despite receiving vehicle injections before being placed into either chamber.
source: Male hindpaw withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired chamber were lower than thresholds recorded in the vehicle-paired chamber on day 4, despite receiving vehicle injections before being placed into either chamber.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Female mice exhibited the same hyperalgesic DCN as males on day 1.
source: Despite exhibiting the same hyperalgesic DCN as males on day 1 (Figure 4C; p < 0.001), female mice exhibited the same level of mechanical sensitivity in the vehicle- and acid-paired contexts on day 4 (Figure 4C, p = 0.81).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and statistical analysis.

claim: Female mice exhibited the same level of mechanical sensitivity in the vehicle- and acid-paired contexts on day 4.
source: Despite exhibiting the same hyperalgesic DCN as males on day 1 (Figure 4C; p < 0.001), female mice exhibited the same level of mechanical sensitivity in the vehicle- and acid-paired contexts on day 4 (Figure 4C, p = 0.81).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and statistical analysis.

claim: Female hindpaw withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired chamber were higher on day 4 than on day 1.
source: Further, in contrast to male mice that exhibited similar withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired chamber on days 1 and 4, female hindpaw withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired chamber were higher on day 4 than on day 1 (p = 0.003), suggesting either a lack of any CR, or the development of conditioned analgesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Naloxone treatment had no effect on the conditioned hypersensitivity exhibited by male mice on day 4.
source: Naloxone treatment had no effect on the conditioned hypersensitivity exhibited by male mice on day 4 (Figure 4E; p = 0.63), further supporting the notion that this behavior is an example of stress-induced hyperalgesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E and statistical analysis.

claim: The conditioned hypersensitivity exhibited by male mice is an example of stress-induced hyperalgesia.
source: Naloxone treatment had no effect on the conditioned hypersensitivity exhibited by male mice on day 4 (Figure 4E; p = 0.63), further supporting the notion that this behavior is an example of stress-induced hyperalgesia.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the naloxone data in males.

claim: When administered in females, naloxone unmasked an endogenous opioid-mediated conditioned compensatory response.
source: When administered in females however, naloxone unmasked an endogenous opioid-mediated conditioned compensatory response (Figure 4E; p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E and statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of naloxone treatment, female behaviors appear to be unaffected by 3 days of acid training.
source: In the absence of naloxone treatment, female behaviors appear to be unaffected by 3 days of acid training (i.e., females had high withdrawal thresholds in the acid-trained context on day 4 relative to day 1 as they did not receive an acetic acid injection prior to entering the context on day 4; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: In the absence of acetic acid injection on day 4, naloxone treatment decreased withdrawal thresholds in females suggesting that females actually exhibit context-dependent conditioned hypersensitivity that is readily counteracted with activation of their endogenous opioid system.
source: However, in the absence of acetic acid injection on day 4, naloxone treatment decreased withdrawal thresholds suggesting that females actually exhibit context-dependent conditioned hypersensitivity that is readily counteracted with activation of their endogenous opioid system.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the naloxone data in females.

claim: Endogenous opioid systems are not engaged by the environment unless that environment is coupled with a painful experience.
source: No main effect of sex, F < 1, drug, F(1, 28) = 2.30, p = 0.14, or an interaction between the two, F(1, 28) = 1.59, p = 0.22 was observed, suggesting that endogenous opioid systems are not engaged by the environment unless that environment is coupled with a painful experience.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the lack of naloxone effects in vehicle-trained animals.

claim: A context (CS) paired with a painful experience (acetic acid injection; UCS) can induce conditioned analgesia in animals upon re-exposure to the CS.
source: We first demonstrated, in a within-subject manner, that a context (CS) paired with a painful experience (acetic acid injection; UCS) can induce conditioned analgesia in animals upon re-exposure to the CS.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Female mice demonstrate conditioned analgesia after pairing a relatively weak UCS with the CS.
source: Although female mice demonstrate this conditioned analgesia after pairing a relatively weak UCS with the CS, male mice only develop conditioned analgesia if a stronger UCS is used throughout conditioning trials.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings comparing Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Male mice only develop conditioned analgesia if a stronger UCS is used throughout conditioning trials.
source: Although female mice demonstrate this conditioned analgesia after pairing a relatively weak UCS with the CS, male mice only develop conditioned analgesia if a stronger UCS is used throughout conditioning trials.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings comparing Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Conditioned analgesia is likely not mediated by stress, but rather by activation of the endogenous opioid system.
source: We then determined that this effect is likely not mediated by stress, but rather by activation of the endogenous opioid system since administration of the opioid antagonist naloxone blocked conditioned analgesia in both sexes.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings from Figure 3.

claim: Males exhibit conditioned hypersensitivity when placed into a context previously associated with pain.
source: In a second set of experiments, we demonstrated that males exhibit conditioned hypersensitivity when placed into a context previously associated with pain.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings from Figure 4B.

claim: Females exhibit conditioned analgesia that is dependent on endogenous opioid signaling when placed into a context previously associated with pain.
source: Alternatively, females exhibit conditioned analgesia that is dependent on endogenous opioid signaling when placed into a similar environment.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings from Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: Context can come to exert control over the endogenous opioid system such that it is recruited as a conditioned compensatory response to ongoing painful stimuli in both sexes.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that context can come to exert control over the endogenous opioid system such that it is recruited as a conditioned compensatory response to ongoing painful stimuli in both sexes, or in anticipation of a painful stimulus in females.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Context can come to exert control over the endogenous opioid system such that it is recruited in anticipation of a painful stimulus in females.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that context can come to exert control over the endogenous opioid system such that it is recruited as a conditioned compensatory response to ongoing painful stimuli in both sexes, or in anticipation of a painful stimulus in females.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Chronic pain may develop, in part, as a result of associative learning.
source: In their 'Imprecision Hypothesis' (2015), Moseley and Vlaeyen posit that chronic pain may develop, in part, as a result of associative learning; repeated coupling of a UCS – in this case a noxious input – with neutral cues like a specific movement of the body (e.g., bending over) or context may lead to the perception of pain (CR) upon subsequent presentation of these newly CS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moseley and Vlaeyen, 2015.

claim: Repeated coupling of a UCS with neutral cues may lead to the perception of pain (CR) upon subsequent presentation of these newly CS.
source: In their 'Imprecision Hypothesis' (2015), Moseley and Vlaeyen posit that chronic pain may develop, in part, as a result of associative learning; repeated coupling of a UCS – in this case a noxious input – with neutral cues like a specific movement of the body (e.g., bending over) or context may lead to the perception of pain (CR) upon subsequent presentation of these newly CS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moseley and Vlaeyen, 2015.

claim: Dimorphisms in endogenous opioid circuit anatomy and function are well documented.
source: Dimorphisms in endogenous opioid circuit anatomy and function are well documented (Chakrabarti et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2007; Loyd and Murphy, 2006; Loyd et al., 2008; Tershner et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the retrosplenial cortex decreases both formalin-associated spontaneous pain and post-surgical mechanical hypersensitivity by modulating opioid signaling in the anterior pretectal nucleus.
source: For example, electrical stimulation of the retrosplenial cortex decreases both formalin-associated spontaneous pain (Reis et al., 2010) and post-surgical mechanical hypersensitivity (Rossaneis et al., 2011) by modulating opioid signaling in the anterior pretectal nucleus (Rossaneis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reis et al., 2010 and Rossaneis et al., 2011.

claim: Women are more sensitive to acute pain stimuli than men.
source: Upon review of this topic, it is clear that women are more sensitive to acute pain stimuli than men, and that chronic pain is more frequently reported in women than it is in men (Mogil, 2012; Mogil, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mogil, 2012 and Mogil, 2020.

claim: Chronic pain is more frequently reported in women than it is in men.
source: Upon review of this topic, it is clear that women are more sensitive to acute pain stimuli than men, and that chronic pain is more frequently reported in women than it is in men (Mogil, 2012; Mogil, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mogil, 2012 and Mogil, 2020.

claim: Female mice exhibited more pain than male mice following low (0.1%) and high (0.9%) acetic acid administration.
source: Rodent data presented in this paper agree with this conclusion; female mice exhibited more pain than male mice following low (0.1%; Figure 1D) and high (0.9%; Figure 2D) acetic acid administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1D and 2D.

claim: Male and ovariectomized female rodents are less sensitive to chemical or mechanical injury of the colon and urinary bladder.
source: Similar quantitative sex differences have been previously reported in other visceral pain models. For example, male and ovariectomized female rodents are less sensitive to chemical or mechanical injury of the colon and urinary bladder (reviewed by Traub and Ji, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Traub and Ji, 2013.

claim: Stronger UCS will support more conditioning to stimuli presented with those UCS.
source: Combined with the fact that stronger UCS will support more conditioning to stimuli presented with those UCS (Holland, 1979; Morris and Bouton, 2006; see Rescorla and Wagner, 1972), the present results suggest that females more readily associate contextual cues with noxious visceral stimuli because they perceive visceral pain more intensely than males.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holland, 1979; Morris and Bouton, 2006; and Rescorla and Wagner, 1972.

claim: Females more readily associate contextual cues with noxious visceral stimuli because they perceive visceral pain more intensely than males.
source: Combined with the fact that stronger UCS will support more conditioning to stimuli presented with those UCS (Holland, 1979; Morris and Bouton, 2006; see Rescorla and Wagner, 1972), the present results suggest that females more readily associate contextual cues with noxious visceral stimuli because they perceive visceral pain more intensely than males.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and cited conditioning principles.

claim: Six of eight female mice exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 2 of the paradigm.
source: In support of this hypothesis, six of eight female mice included in Figure 2 exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 2 of the paradigm (i.e., higher paw withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired chamber on day 2 vs. day 1) whereas zero of the eight male mice in this same study exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zero of the eight male mice exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 2.
source: In support of this hypothesis, six of eight female mice included in Figure 2 exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 2 of the paradigm (i.e., higher paw withdrawal thresholds in the acid-paired chamber on day 2 vs. day 1) whereas zero of the eight male mice in this same study exhibited conditioned analgesia on day 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A wide variety of internal states have been shown to serve as contextual stimuli that influence behavioral performance.
source: A wide variety of internal states have been shown to serve as contextual stimuli that influence behavioral performance (Garfinkel et al., 2021; Schepers and Bouton, 2017; Schepers and Bouton, 2019; see Bouton, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: After one pairing of 0.9% acetic acid and context, male mice exhibit conditioned hypersensitivity.
source: For example, after one pairing of 0.9% acetic acid and context, male mice exhibit conditioned hypersensitivity (Martin et al., 2019) whereas females, based on the observations made in these studies, likely exhibit conditioned analgesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2019.

claim: After one pairing of 0.9% acetic acid and context, females likely exhibit conditioned analgesia.
source: For example, after one pairing of 0.9% acetic acid and context, male mice exhibit conditioned hypersensitivity (Martin et al., 2019) whereas females, based on the observations made in these studies, likely exhibit conditioned analgesia.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from the current study.

claim: Previous exposure to a putative CS makes it more difficult to become predictive of a UCS (termed 'latent inhibition').
source: It is a well-documented finding that previous exposure to a putative CS makes it more difficult to become predictive of a UCS (termed 'latent inhibition'; e.g., Lubow, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lubow, 1973.

claim: C57BL/6 mice aged 8–12 weeks were used in all experiments.
source: Equally sized cohorts of male and female C57BL/6 mice aged 8–12 weeks were used in all experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mice were either bred in house or purchased from The Jackson Laboratory.
source: Mice were either bred in house or purchased from The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME).
evidence: This is a methodological detail stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Purchased animals acclimated to the housing facility for >7 days before experimental use.
source: Purchased animals acclimated to the housing facility for >7 days before experimental use.
evidence: This is a methodological detail stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All protocols were in accordance with National Institute of Health guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the Medical College of Wisconsin.
source: All protocols were in accordance with National Institute of Health guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the Medical College of Wisconsin (Milwaukee, WI; protocol #0383).
evidence: This is a methodological detail stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Repeated acetic acid injections as painful stimuli were previously used in Stevenson et al., 2006.
source: We are not the first to use repeated acetic acid injections as painful stimuli. This procedure was previously used in Stevenson et al., 2006; approximately 4 hr after acetic acid injection, animals no longer exhibited acetic acid-induced feeding suppression in those studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stevenson et al., 2006.

claim: Approximately 4 hr after acetic acid injection, animals no longer exhibited acetic acid-induced feeding suppression.
source: We are not the first to use repeated acetic acid injections as painful stimuli. This procedure was previously used in Stevenson et al., 2006; approximately 4 hr after acetic acid injection, animals no longer exhibited acetic acid-induced feeding suppression in those studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stevenson et al., 2006.

claim: No animal in the study lost more than 15% of their body weight over the course of the experiments.
source: Similarly, no animal in our study lost more than 15% of their body weight over the course of the experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological observation stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The 0.9% dose of acetic acid was used as the final UCS since it has previously been shown to elicit conditioned pain hypersensitivity in male mice.
source: The 0.9% dose of acetic acid was used as the final UCS since it has previously been shown to elicit conditioned pain hypersensitivity in male mice (Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2019.

claim: The dose of naloxone (10 mg/kg) has previously been shown to block the contribution of endogenous opioid signaling in the tail-withdrawal test.
source: This dose (10 mg/kg) has previously been shown to block the contribution of endogenous opioid signaling in the tail-withdrawal test (Rosen et al., 2019) and reduce spontaneous pain behaviors initiated by complete Freund's adjuvant injection (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rosen et al., 2019.

claim: The dose of naloxone (10 mg/kg) has previously been shown to reduce spontaneous pain behaviors initiated by complete Freund's adjuvant injection.
source: This dose (10 mg/kg) has previously been shown to block the contribution of endogenous opioid signaling in the tail-withdrawal test (Rosen et al., 2019) and reduce spontaneous pain behaviors initiated by complete Freund's adjuvant injection (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claim: The phenomenon called 'anti-DNIC', facilitatory CPM, or 'hyperalgesic DCN' is observed across multiple rodent species and mouse strains and does not depend on the anatomical proximity of the injured and test sites.
source: In contrast to the 'pain-inhibits-pain' idea associated with the electrophysiological phenomenon known as DNIC, this observation which has been called 'anti-DNIC', facilitatory CPM, or 'hyperalgesic DCN' is observed across multiple rodent species and mouse strains and does not depend on the anatomical proximity of the injured and test sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tansley et al., 2019.
